item.title: Organizing for the future – how do OSCM processes and organization design need to evolve in the wake of technological and/or geopolitical disruptions?
item.content:encoded:
Lydia Bals, Mainz University of Applied Sciences

Virpi Turkulainen, Haaga-Helia University of Applied Sciences

Organization design has been proposed to be contingent upon a broad spectrum of external and internal factors since the 1960s. Recent developments in technologies and geopolitical landscape offer a timely and important research area. Novel perspectives are needed on how processes and organization designs in operations and supply chain management (OSCM) are changing. Both sound theoretical base and appropriate methodology should drive novel perspectives on how OSCM processes and organization designs are evolving. Novel insights can pertain to the domain, the variables, variable relationships as well as predicted outcomes.

The acceleration of digitalization and new technologies has the potential to support better decision making by eliminating biases and allowing pooling of more information, yet it has increased the complexity of managing supply chains. There is now a need to share assets and information that were not considered appropriate to share before, and new types of alliances and agreements need to be created. From self-service procurement and autonomous buying to sourcing strategies and artificial intelligence utilization for data analytics, procurement departments are being digitized through new applications, smart platforms and pilot projects.

Geopolitics also increase the complexity of managing global supply chains. The global semiconductor market exemplifies this, with the majority of global semiconductor production concentrated in Taiwan, with microchips production reaching even over 90%. Recent shortages in electricity have forced factory closures globally in various sectors, making it evident that extreme global dependency on a very limited number of actors in today's geopolitical context poses severe consequences.

OSCM is at the crossroads: it can either embrace such disruptions proactively or react to them passively. New emerging technologies and changing geopolitical context force OSCM to reconsider how to adapt. Two main responses to the changes are management of the processes and organization design, aligning organizational considerations with the process landscape. Contingency theory and information processing theory are helpful theoretical underpinnings for research in this area. Contingency theory accounts for the relationship between organization design and internal or external factors such as size, strategy, and uncertainties in the task environment. Information processing theory proposes that an organization's design with its information processing capacity should fit the organization's need for information. These theories have been applied in the OSCM field to examine how different procurement organizational structures facilitate information processing capacity or how various factors affect production location decisions in high cost countries. The question remains whether these considerations hold true under the changed contextual conditions of our times and whether new variables need to update previous theoretical work.

In response to recent disruptions such as COVID-19 and the US-China trade war, companies have developed supply chain structural ambidexterity, referring to dual structures with separate roles. Work that proposes how disruptions are affecting strategic shifts in business models and subsequent adaptations to the organization design of OSCM functions would be relevant. This follows the idea that structure follows strategy. How to organize OSCM functions might need to change in the wake of new requirements; what might have been effective and efficient ways to manage and organize these functions traditionally might be less so in times of AI utilization, autonomous processes, current wars, and new trade barriers.

Potential topics

  • OSCM processes: implications of emerging technologies and geopolitical disruptions on different aspects of OSCM processes, such as how absorptive capacity influences technology adoption, or how specific new technologies (e.g., regenerative AI, additive manufacturing, blockchain) or new regulations affect supply network dynamics
  • OSCM organization design: incorporating technologies and geopolitics as contingency factors in models of organization design, managing division of tasks and coordination of work between IT and supply chain, operations, procurement and logistics functions, moving beyond human-centric organization designs toward designing systems composed of human and non-human knowledge workers, understanding how geopolitical disruptions affect organization design aspects on a global scale
  • Technology-based decision-making: understanding factors affecting division of labor between humans and AI, coordinating work between technology and humans as decision-makers, integrating robot bosses into OSCM processes
  • Competence development: identifying competences OSCM personnel need considering emerging technologies, understanding critical situations that OSCM professionals need to cope with

Timeline

  • February 1, 2026: Closing date for abstract/proposal submission
  • March 1, 2026: Opening date for manuscript submissions
  • October 31, 2026: Closing date for manuscript submission

item.title: From Individuals to Organizations: Unpacking Behavioral Issues in Supply Chain Risk Management
item.content:encoded:
Jon F. Kirchoff, East Carolina University

Ying Liao, East Carolina University

Shingirai Chris Kwaramba, Virginia Commonwealth University

At its core, supply chain risk management (SCRM) research has focused on identifying and assessing known and unknown risks, and on risk mitigation to derive and implement solutions that ensure supply will continue to meet demand during and after a disruptive event. However, supply chain disruptions have been escalating in recent years and revealed considerable complex vulnerabilities in how firms manage their global operations. Current SCRM strategies, theories, and frameworks are ill-equipped to address these vulnerabilities, despite years of experience and research.

A justified concern in the literature is that the assumptions of risk neutrality and rationality of decision-makers is unrealistic. In reality, supply chain decision-makers fall along a broad spectrum from risk seeking to risk aversion and often make decisions under bounded rationality and are influenced by cognitive biases and other factors that cause them to deviate from optimal or rational choices, especially under conditions of uncertainty, tension, and time pressure. Deviations from rationality influence risk identification, assessment, and mitigation, leading to a gap between theoretical predictions and actual supply chain outcomes. Ignoring behavioral realities leads to suboptimal risk management strategies, reduced operational efficiency and profitability. Thus, the behavioral aspect is crucial in determining whether supply chains recover or remain fragile in the face of disruption.

Research on the behavioral and non-rational aspects of supply chain risk management has been primarily at the individual level such as human cognition, biases, interpersonal relationship, individualism, confidence level, personal wealth and regulatory focus. However, little attention has been devoted to how individual behavior is shaped by organizational and inter-organizational factors such as risk appetite, dependency and power asymmetries, and the adoption of industry 4.0 technologies. Therefore, research on behavioral issues in supply chain risk management needs to be researched across the individual decision making-level (micro), the entity decision making-level (macro), and the supply chain decision making-level (interorganizational).

This perspective also requires investigating how decisions by one actor (individual, team, or organization) cascade systematically influence others, both within an organization and across the broader supply chain network. Drawing on insights from psychology, behavioral theories, decision-making frameworks, organizational studies, and risk management frameworks, this special issue seeks to unpack these behavioral dimensions to advance a holistic understanding of SCRM.

This call for papers focuses on behavioral issues in supply chain risk management, across multiple levels. In line with the journal's aim to advance theoretical concepts and frameworks and given this call's focus on unpacking behavioral issues in supply chain risk management, we are particularly interested in research that explores the limitations of existing theories in the literature and/or research that introduces new and innovative concepts and frameworks that address the complexities of supply chain risk management.

Potential topics

  • To what extent does strategic manipulation of information (withholding, distorting, or framing risk signals) affect collective supply chain resilience outcomes?
  • How can behavioral theories explain inter-firm risk-sharing under uncertainty?
  • How can interdisciplinary (i.e. psychology, sociology) perspectives be used to explain multi-level intention action reaction dynamics in risk situations spanning individuals, organizations and supply chains?
  • How do individual decision-making styles aggregate into organizational risk cultures and capabilities?
  • How do behavioral dynamics across levels (micro, macro, interorganizational) complement or contradict one another in shaping supply chain resilience?
  • What mechanisms explain how individual-level behaviors (e.g., bounded rationality, trust, or opportunism) cascade into network-level collaboration or conflict in supply chain risk management?
  • What are the unintended consequences when human intuition and AI recommendations diverge in supply chain risk management decisions?
  • To what extent do fear appeals, regulatory pressures, or organizational risk cultures motivate or inhibit proactive cyber risk management?
  • How do disruptive technologies impact behavior?

Timeline

  • March 15, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • April 15, 2026: Closing date for abstract submission
  • September 15, 2026: Closing date for manuscripts submission
